To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
pigeons preferred a fixed-time schedule over a fixed-interval schedule when the fixed-interval was segmented into two or more shorter components.

pigeons preferred the tandem to the chained fixed-interval schedule when both schedules contained a 5-s fixed-time component, and that the preference for the tandem schedule increased with increasing length of the chained schedule.

pigeons prefer the tandem over the segmented chained fixed-time 5 s schedule in the terminal-link schedule, and that preference for the tandem schedule increases as the first component in the chained fixed-time schedule increases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of segmentation of a fixed-time schedule on concurrent choice.
the effect on choice of the temporal structure of a schedule component, and the effect of the presence and absence of a stimulus change at the beginning of a schedule component.
a comparison between the tandem and chained fixed-interval schedules of reinforcement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
preference for the tandem schedule over the chained schedule is not a reliable effect.

preference for a tandem over a chained schedule is a function of the number of segments, the length of the segments, and the presence or absence of a stimulus that signals reinforcement in the chained schedule.
preference for less segmented schedules is not always evident in concurrent-chain procedures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
preference for less segmented schedules in the terminal link is dependent upon the presence of a stimulus in the first component and upon the length of that component.
preference for the tandem schedule is not a function of signaling the onset of the first component, but is a function of the relative length of the first and second components.
pigeons prefer less segmented response-independent components, but only when the first component is short.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pigeons prefer less segmented schedules of reinforcement.
preference for less segmented components of a schedule of reinforcement can be obtained even when the terminal link contains a tandem schedule of reinforcement.
pigeons' preference for the less segmented fixed-time schedule was not influenced by the presence of a stimulus change at the onset of the fixed-time component.
